planting.note: Plant bare-root or potted suckers in early spring before bud break into deep, well-drained soil.

directions: Smoky is one of the oldest named saskatoon selections, prized for consistent heavy fruiting and reliably sweet, dark purple berries on a suckering multi-stem shrub. It tolerates extreme prairie winters and thrives in a wide range of soils provided drainage is adequate. Thin out old canes periodically to keep the clump productive and encourage new fruiting wood.

planting.note: Set out dormant nursery stock in early spring in full sun, spacing plants for eventual clump width.

directions: Martin produces some of the largest berries among the older Alberta-origin saskatoon selections, with a vigorous upright growth habit that suits both hedgerow and orchard-row plantings. Fruit clusters ripen fairly uniformly, making a single hand-harvest practical for home growers. Established plants sucker readily, so allow room for the clump to widen over time.

planting.note: Plant in early spring in full sun on well-drained ground; group two or more clumps for best cross-pollination and fruit set.

directions: Pembina was selected in North Dakota for its earlier ripening window compared to many prairie saskatoon cultivars, giving gardeners in short-season regions a head start on the harvest. The shrub forms a dense, rounded multi-stem clump with reliable annual bloom and good resistance to late spring frosts at flowering. Renewal-prune a portion of the oldest canes each winter to keep fruiting wood vigorous.

planting.note: Root hardwood cuttings or plant container stock in fall or very early spring in moist, humus-rich soil with some afternoon shade in hot climates.

directions: Primus is a classic Dutch white currant selection valued for its long, evenly filled strigs of translucent, pale gold berries with a milder, less acidic flavor than red currants. It is largely self-fertile and productive on a compact, upright bush, making it a good choice for smaller garden beds or espalier training. Mulch to keep roots cool and moist through summer, and prune out the oldest wood each winter to maintain strong new fruiting shoots.

subcategory: Eastern Filbert Blight-resistant OSU hazelnut cultivar

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees while dormant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and pair with Jefferson or Yamhill for pollination.

directions: Wepster is one of the Oregon State University hazelnut releases bred to withstand Eastern Filbert Blight, functioning primarily as a reliable pollenizer for later-blooming EFB-resistant varieties like Jefferson and Yamhill. It forms a moderately vigorous, well-branched bush that begins bearing within a few years of planting. Because hazelnuts are wind-pollinated and self-incompatible, always plant it alongside a compatible bloom-overlap partner rather than as a stand-alone tree.

subcategory: thin-shelled, easy-cracking named black walnut cultivar

planting.note: Plant grafted trees while dormant in deep, well-drained soil away from garden beds, since black walnut roots exude growth-inhibiting juglone.

directions: Emma K is a widely propagated named black walnut selection valued by home nut growers for its comparatively thin shell and high percentage of easily removed kernel meat relative to typical wild seedling trees. Grafted trees bear considerably sooner and more consistently than seedling-grown black walnuts. Give it wide open spacing away from vegetable gardens and susceptible landscape plants due to juglone sensitivity in nearby soil.
sources: University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry

planting.note: Plant grafted trees while dormant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil with full sun exposure and ample room to mature.

directions: Sparrow is a long-cultivated named black walnut selection recognized among nut growers for producing unusually large nuts with good kernel fill for the species. Like other grafted black walnut cultivars, it bears years earlier than seedling trees and produces more uniform crops. Deep taproots make bare-root or containerized grafted stock the practical planting choice, and trees should be sited well clear of gardens sensitive to juglone.
sources: University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry

planting.note: Plant grafted or seedling trees in well-drained, slightly acidic soil, with a second genetically distinct chestnut nearby for pollination.

directions: Gideon is a Chinese chestnut selection notable for its cold hardiness well beyond the range where most Chinese chestnut cultivars perform reliably, making it a favored parent tree and orchard choice in colder northern climates. It bears a good crop of medium nuts with the sweet, easy-peeling qualities typical of Chinese chestnut. Chestnuts are self-incompatible, so plant at least two unrelated seedlings or cultivars within pollination range for consistent nut set.
sources: University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry
